extracted.intended_audience: applicant organizations, authorized organizational officials (AORs), principal investigators, and institutional grant administrators applying for or receiving NIH funding
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards institutions and investigators must follow to be eligible for, receive, and conduct NIH-funded research (human subjects protections, reporting, training, monitoring, regulatory compliance, and public policy requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior IRB approval and human subjects funding restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not draw funds from the payment system, request funds from the paying office, or make obligations against Federal funds for research involving human subjects at any site engaged in nonexempt research for any period not covered by both an FWA and IRB approval consistent with 45 CFR Part 46.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs associated with IRB review of human research protocols are not allowable as direct charges to NIH-funded research unless such costs are not covered by the organization’s indirect cost rate. The use of autopsy materials is governed by applicable State and local law and is not regulated by 45 CFR Part 46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalwide Assurance (FWA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each institution engaged in HHS-supported human subjects research must be covered by an FWA approved by OHRP. When an applicant proposes nonexempt human subjects research and does not have an FWA, the AOR signature constitutes a declaration that the organization will comply with 45 CFR Part 46 and proceed to obtain an FWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH will place a restriction in the NoA so that no human subjects research may be conducted until the FWA and certification of IRB review and approval (or certification of exemption) have been obtained and accepted by NIH. Each recipient institution must file its own FWA even if it designates another IRB. IRBs must be registered with OHRP before being designated on an FWA. Additional performance sites engaged in nonexempt research must obtain an FWA or, under specified circumstances, may be covered by the recipient's FWA per OHRP guidance. The recipient organization is responsible for ensuring all sites engaged in human subjects research are covered by an appropriate FWA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation/sponsorship requirement for individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: No individual may receive NIH grant funds for nonexempt research involving human subjects unless the individual is affiliated with or sponsored by an organization that assumes responsibility for the research under an FWA or the individual makes other arrangements with OHRP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed information about FWAs is available on the OHRP website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of IRB approval (final approval date required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide a certification to NIH that all nonexempt human subjects research has been reviewed and approved by an appropriate IRB, consistent with 45 CFR Part 46 and OHRP guidance. NIH requires the date of final IRB approval; conditional IRB approval is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH-funded U.S. sites cannot rely on a non‑U.S. IRB. For delayed-onset human subjects research, prior to involvement of subjects the recipient must submit detailed Human Subjects and Clinical Trials information and the certification and date of final IRB approval to the awarding IC. Certification may be filed via Just-in-Time unless the IC requires earlier submission. Under no circumstances may nonexempt human subjects research be initiated prior to obtaining IRB approval and providing the final IRB approval date to NIH. Changes to protocols or addition of new protocols that were peer reviewed require prior approval of the NIH awarding IC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting unanticipated problems, noncompliance, suspensions/terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient institutions must establish and follow written procedures for prompt reporting to the IRB, institutional officials, and NIH of any unanticipated problems involving risks to subjects or others; any serious or continuing noncompliance with 45 CFR Part 46 or IRB requirements; and any suspension or termination of IRB approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any IRB suspension or termination must include a statement of reasons and be reported promptly to the investigator, institutional officials, and NIH (45 CFR Part 46.113). Institutions must also file incident reports promptly with OHRP of unanticipated problems, serious or continuing noncompliance, and suspensions/terminations. See OHRP's Guidance on Reporting Incidents to OHRP for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: OHRP oversight and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: OHRP has regulatory responsibility for oversight of recipient compliance with HHS human subjects regulations and evaluates written allegations or indications of non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective actions are tailored to remedy identified non-compliance and prevent reoccurrence; most are resolved at OHRP but OHRP may recommend actions to other HHS officials. Information about FWA submission, oversight activities, and copies of human subjects regulations are available from OHRP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education in the protection of human research participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Before funds are awarded for competing applications involving human subjects, applicants must submit documentation that all senior/key personnel involved in human subjects research have received training in the protection of human subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior/key personnel include all individuals responsible for design or conduct, including senior/key personnel at all sites. Documentation should be included in the AOR-signed cover letter accompanying Just-in-Time materials (other support, IRB/IACUC approval). For non-competing continuation awards, education for new senior/key personnel should be part of the progress report. Additional information available on NIH's Training & Resources – Human Subjects page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and safety monitoring requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH policy requires oversight and monitoring of all NIH-conducted or -supported human biomedical and behavioral intervention studies (clinical trials) to ensure participant safety and data integrity, with monitoring level/frequency commensurate with risks, nature, size, and complexity of the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring options include PD/PI (required), IRB (required), independent safety officer, designated medical/research monitor, internal committee/board with guidelines, and DSMB (required for multi-site trials). Applications with clinical trials must include a general description of the monitoring plan (reviewed by the SRG); a detailed monitoring plan must be part of the protocol, submitted to the IRB, and reviewed/approved by the awarding IC prior to accrual. DSMBs are specifically required for multi-site clinical trials involving interventions with potential risk and generally for Phase III trials. For multi-site Phase I/II trials, organize a central reporting entity for timely adverse event summaries. DSMB summary reports should be forwarded to each responsible IRB. See SF424 (R&R) instructions section G.500 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion across the lifespan (age inclusion policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all competing grant applications, individuals of all ages (including children under 18 and older adults 65+) must be included in human subjects research unless there are scientific or ethical reasons not to include them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must address age-appropriate inclusion/exclusion and include a rationale for chosen age range. Scientific review groups will assess each application as 'acceptable' or 'unacceptable' for age‑appropriate inclusion/exclusion. NIH staff will monitor implementation; recipients must submit participant age at enrollment in progress reports. Investigators should design studies so de-identified individual-level participant data on sex, race, ethnicity, and age at enrollment may be provided to NIH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of women and racial/ethnic minority groups
rubrics_metrics.description: All NIH-funded or supported clinical research must address inclusion of women and members of racial and/or ethnic minority groups (and subgroups), developing a research design appropriate to the scientific objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The research plan should describe proposed study population composition by sex and race/ethnicity and provide a rationale for selection; plan outreach/recruitment activities. Exceptions may be granted by an IC/ICO Director (or NIH Director on recommendation) with compelling justification; cost is not an acceptable reason for exclusion except when inclusion would duplicate existing data. Women of childbearing potential should not be routinely excluded. For NIH-defined Phase III clinical trials, investigators must consider sex/race/ethnicity differences and for applicable trials specify and report outcomes and valid analyses by sex and/or ethnicity in ClinicalTrials.gov. Investigators must collect and annually report sex, race, and ethnicity using OMB Directive No. 15 standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH expects all NIH-funded investigators and staff involved in the conduct, oversight, or management of clinical trials to be trained in Good Clinical Practice (GCP), consistent with ICH E6 (R3) principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCP training demonstrates fundamental knowledge of clinical trial quality standards (designing, conducting, recording, reporting). Training may be via class/course, academic program, or certification from recognized organizations. GCP training should be refreshed at least every three years. Recipients are expected to retain documentation of training and make it available to NIH upon request. Definitions provided for 'Investigator' and 'clinical trial staff' clarify covered personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single IRB (sIRB) requirement for domestic multi-site research
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH requires U.S. sites engaged in NIH-funded multi-site research conducted at more than one domestic site to rely upon approval by a single Institutional Review Board (sIRB) as required by the Revised Common Rule and NIH sIRB policy (initial IRB approval on or after January 20, 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH expects the domestic sites to rely on a U.S. sIRB; foreign sites are not expected to use a single IRB. Applicants subject to sIRB requirements must provide the sIRB name during Just-in-Time before award; for delayed-onset research, provide sIRB name to the IC prior to initiating the study. Applicants may request direct cost funding for sIRB establishment/review with justification; costs must be reasonable and consistent with cost principles. Recipients must ensure authorization agreements are in place and maintain documentation. Participating sites are expected to rely on the sIRB for regulatory IRB review; institutions may perform additional local review but that is not the regulatory review and NIH funds may not be used to pay for duplicate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: IND/IDE and FDA compliance for trials involving regulated products
rubrics_metrics.description: All clinical research involving investigational drugs, devices, or other FDA‑regulated products must comply with all applicable FDA requirements (INDs, IDEs) and human subjects protections (21 CFR Parts 50, 56, 312, 812).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IND/IDE sponsor (NIH, recipient, or third party) is legally responsible for meeting FDA sponsor requirements. The recipient is ultimately responsible to NIH for ensuring compliance. After filing an IND, FDA has 30 days to review and may allow, defer, suspend, or terminate. When NIH funds any part of a study involving an IND/IDE, the recipient must report certain FDA communications to the NIH awarding IC within 72 hours of receiving or being informed of them (e.g., warning letters; Notices of Initiation of Disqualification Proceedings; Notice of Opportunity for Hearing; Notice of Disqualification; Consent Agreements; clinical hold letters that pertain to breaches of GMP, GCP, or major protocol issues). Notification should be in writing but may be by telephone if writing would delay notification. Failure to comply may result in corrective/enforcement action. FDA communications are grant-related records subject to retention and access rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying prohibition and required certifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients of Federal grants, cooperative agreements, contracts, and loans are prohibited under 31 U.S.C. 1352 and 45 CFR Part 93 from using appropriated Federal funds to influence or attempt to influence federal officers, employees, or Members of Congress regarding awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must certify and disclose that they: (1) have not made and will not make prohibited payments; (2) used or will use non-appropriated funds if they have made such payments; and (3) will include these requirements in consortium agreements and contracts under grants exceeding $100,000 and obtain necessary certifications from those participants/contractors. Certifications and disclosures must be filed at times prescribed based on expected total costs. The AOR's signature on the application serves as the required certification of compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric system usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with EO 12770, measurement values in applications and recipient-prepared reports, publications, and other grant-related documents should be in metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Construction Grants chapter in IIB for metric requirements specific to construction activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military recruiting / ROTC access eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 588 of the NDAA (10 U.S.C. §983) precludes NIH grant awards to institutions of higher education that DoD determines have an anti-ROTC policy or practice that prevents the Secretary of Defense from gaining entry to campuses or access to students or information for military recruiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DoD publishes determinations of ineligibility in the Federal Register and a semiannual list of ineligible schools. If DoD determines an institution is ineligible during an ongoing project period, NIH will suspend support of current and future grant awards per enforcement rules. Funding eligibility may be restored based on new information provided by DoD.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA environmental impact notification and categorical exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: All NIH grants are subject to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Recipients are required to promptly notify NIH of any reasonably foreseeable environmental impacts from grant-supported activities, or certify that no such impacts will arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH has determined that most research grants will not have significant environmental effects unless the proposed research includes one or more of listed categorical concerns (e.g., scope/size greater than category actions; threatens to violate environmental law; unique/highly uncertain effects; use of especially hazardous substances without known controls; may overload waste treatment plants; possible impact on endangered species; introduce new hazardous/toxic wastes or require storage pending disposal technology; introduce new sources of radiation; substantial and reasonable controversy about environmental effects). This requirement supplements other public policy requirements for construction and A&R activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondelinquency on federal debt certification
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization or individual indebted to the United States with a judgment lien filed against it is ineligible to receive a Federal grant; the AOR must certify that the organization (or individual for certain fellowships) is not delinquent in repaying any Federal debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If delinquent, NIH may not award the grant until debt is satisfied or satisfactory arrangements made; once satisfied NIH will consider delinquency when determining responsibility. Individuals in default with a judgment lien should not be listed as participants until satisfied; no funds may be used to pay such an individual. NIH will disallow costs charged to awards that provide funds to individuals in violation of this Act. These requirements apply to all organization types and foreign grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: PEPFAR prostitution and sex trafficking provision
rubrics_metrics.description: All grants awarded under PEPFAR include specific terms prohibiting use of funds to promote or advocate legalization or practice of prostitution or sex trafficking; the U.S. Government is opposed to prostitution and related activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision states exceptions for provision of palliative care, treatment, post-exposure prophylaxis, necessary pharmaceuticals and commodities (including test kits, condoms, and, when proven effective, microbicides). It defines 'commercial sex act', 'prostitution', and 'sex trafficking' for the provision. The recipient must insert this standard provision in all subawards/subcontracts. Violation of the provision is grounds for unilateral termination of the award by NIH prior to the end of its term.
